claim: During embryogenesis tissue layers undergo morphogenetic flow rearranging and folding into specific shapes.
source: During embryogenesis tissue layers undergo morphogenetic flow rearranging and folding into specific shapes.
evidence: This is a general statement about embryogenesis that draws from established scientific knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: The complex spatio-temporal flow pattern can be predicted from the measured meso-scale myosin density and anisotropy using a simple, effective viscous model of the tissue, achieving close to 90% accuracy with one time dependent and two constant parameters.
source: We find that the complex spatio-temporal flow pattern can be predicted from the measured meso-scale myosin density and anisotropy using a simple, effective viscous model of the tissue, achieving close to 90% accuracy with one time dependent and two constant parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3 showing the fit residuals and predicted vs measured flow fields.

claim: Spatial modulation of myosin distribution on the scale of the embryo is important for morphogenetic flow.
source: Our analysis uncovers the importance of a) spatial modulation of myosin distribution on the scale of the embryo and b) the non-locality of its effect due to mechanical interaction of cells, demonstrating the need for the global perspective in the study of morphogenetic flow.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and in silico perturbations shown in Figure 4d demonstrating the effects of removing spatial modulation.

claim: The non-locality of myosin's effect due to mechanical interaction of cells is important for morphogenetic flow.
source: Our analysis uncovers the importance of a) spatial modulation of myosin distribution on the scale of the embryo and b) the non-locality of its effect due to mechanical interaction of cells, demonstrating the need for the global perspective in the study of morphogenetic flow.
evidence: This is supported by the continuum mechanics modeling approach and the demonstration that local myosin perturbations have global effects on flow patterns.

claim: The Drosophila embryonic blastoderm is an epithelial monolayer of about 6000 cells on the surface of the embryo.
source: During gastrulation of Drosophila, for example, the embryonic blastoderm – an epithelial monolayer of about 6000 cells on the surface of the embryo – undergoes a dramatic deformation that changes tissue topology and gives rise to the three germ layers.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in Drosophila developmental biology.

claim: Ventral furrow formation involves apical constriction of presumptive mesoderm cells.
source: Live imaging has also uncovered process-specific cell behaviors such as apical constriction of presumptive mesoderm cells during ventral furrow formation (Martin et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Martin et al., 2009.

claim: Germ-band extension involves intercalation of neighboring cells in the lateral ectoderm.
source: Live imaging has also uncovered process-specific cell behaviors such as apical constriction of presumptive mesoderm cells during ventral furrow formation (Martin et al., 2009) and intercalation of neighboring cells in the lateral ectoderm during convergent extension (Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Bertet et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004 and Bertet et al., 2004.

claim: Cell behaviors during gastrulation are associated with localized activity of the force generating non-muscle myosin II.
source: These behaviors are associated with localized activity of the force generating non-muscle myosin II (Martin et al., 2009; Irvine and Wieschaus, 1994; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Bertet et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Tissue remodeling during Drosophila gastrulation is characterized by three simple flow field configurations.
source: Using optical flow velocimetry applied to cylinder projections of the Surface of Interest (SOI) passing through cells below the apical cell surface (see SI for details Figure 1—figure supplement 5c), we find that tissue remodeling during Drosophila gastrulation is characterized by three simple flow field configurations (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optical flow velocimetry data shown in Figure 1c-e.

claim: The earliest flows start well before the ventral furrow forms, and are characterized by a dorsal sink and ventral source.
source: The earliest flows start well before the ventral furrow (VF) forms, and are characterized by a dorsal sink and ventral source (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow field data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: During pre-VF flow, no cells are internalized, but rather cells reduce cross section on the dorsal side.
source: In contrast to the VF, no cells are internalized during this flow, but rather cells reduce cross section on the dorsal side (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: As the VF forms, source and sink swap sides and a large group of cells internalize on the ventral side, as mesoderm precursors leave the surface of the blastoderm.
source: As the VF forms, source and sink swap sides and a large group of cells internalize on the ventral side, as mesoderm precursors leave the surface of the blastoderm (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow field data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: During germband extension, the flow pattern exhibits two saddles arranged on the dorsal and ventral sides as well as four vortices, two in the posterior and two in the anterior end.
source: During germband extension (GBE), the flow pattern exhibits two saddles arranged on the dorsal and ventral sides as well as four vortices, two in the posterior and two in the anterior end (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow field data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The pre-VF flow associates with basal myosin that exhibits a pronounced Dorso Ventral asymmetry, with high levels of myosin on the dorsal and low levels on the ventral side.
source: The pre-VF flow associates with basal myosin that exhibits a pronounced Dorso Ventral (DV) asymmetry (Warn et al., 1980; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Polyakov et al., 2014), with high levels of myosin on the dorsal and low levels on the ventral side (Figure 1f)
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in Figure 1f and citations to prior work.

claim: During pre-VF flow, the apical myosin pool appears uniform across the surface.
source: The pre-VF flow associates with basal myosin that exhibits a pronounced Dorso Ventral (DV) asymmetry (Warn et al., 1980; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Polyakov et al., 2014), with high levels of myosin on the dorsal and low levels on the ventral side (Figure 1f), while the apical pool appears uniform across the surface (Figure 1i, Figure 1—figure supplement 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 5d–g.

claim: The basal myosin pool remains asymmetric during VF flow.
source: The basal pool remains asymmetric during VF flow (Figure 1g)
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: During VF flow, the apical myosin pool develops DV asymmetry in reversed orientation compared to the basal pool.
source: The basal pool remains asymmetric during VF flow (Figure 1g), but the apical pool now also develops DV asymmetry in reversed orientation (Figure 1j).
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: The asymmetry on the apical surface becomes further pronounced in the GBE-phase.
source: The asymmetry on the apical surface becomes further pronounced in the GBE-phase (Figure 1h,k, Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in Figure 1h,k and Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Global changes in myosin pools are a hallmark for transitions in flow field configuration.
source: Global changes in myosin pools are a hallmark for transitions in flow field configuration (Figure 2a, Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2, 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of myosin pools shown in Figure 2a and related supplementary figures.

claim: Myosin is initially enriched in the basal pool, and as sink and source swap position, it begins to accumulate on the apical side.
source: Myosin is initially enriched in the basal pool, and as sink and source swap position, it begins to accumulate on the apical side.
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of myosin pools shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Cortical myosin on the apical cell surface polarizes during convergent extension.
source: While the basal pool is isotropic (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a), cortical myosin on the apical cell surface is known to polarize during convergent extension (Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004; Bertet et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The anisotropic signal in the apical pool starts out low, but increases from about 8 min corresponding to late stage 6.
source: The anisotropic signal in the apical pool starts out low, but increases from about 8 min corresponding to late stage 6 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 4b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 4b,c.

claim: The anisotropy axis aligns well with local tangent to pair rule gene expression boundaries.
source: The anisotropy axis, readily computed by the eigenvectors of the myosin tensor, aligns well with local tangent to pair rule gene expression boundaries (Figure 2a,d, Figure 2—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of myosin anisotropy axes with pair-rule gene expression patterns shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Anisotropies are thought to be driven by the patterned juxtaposition of pair-rule gene expression.
source: This is the expected result given that anisotropies are thought to be driven by the patterned juxtaposition of pair-rule gene expression (Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004.

claim: The model achieves about 90% accurate description of the flow pattern before and after VF invagination.
source: Even without spatial modulation of the parameters, the model achieves about 90% accurate description of the flow pattern before and after VF invagination (see Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fit residual analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The main discrepancy of model predictions for pre-VF flow is a displacement of sink and source positions along the AP axis by less than 30 µm.
source: The main discrepancy of model predictions for pre-VF flow (see Figure 3c) is a displacement of sink and source positions along the AP axis by less than 30 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of predicted and measured flow fields shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Prediction of GBE flow essentially agrees with measurements across the entire embryo, with the exception of a domain close to the vortices on the posterior end.
source: Prediction of GBE flow essentially agrees with measurements across the entire embryo, with the exception of a domain close to the vortices on the posterior end, due to a mismatch of fixed-point location (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of predicted and measured flow fields shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The model correctly predicts subtle differences between anterior and posterior fixed points along the DV axis.
source: Remarkably, our model is even able to correctly predict subtle differences between anterior and posterior fixed points along the DV axis (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of predicted and measured flow fields shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Before and during VF invagination cells are less resistant to surface area compression than during GBE.
source: Measured flow is first dominated by sources and sinks that disappear later during GBE, suggesting that before and during VF invagination cells are less resistant to surface area compression than during GBE.
evidence: This is inferred from the flow field topology and the changes in the ratio of viscosities shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The ν2/ν1 ratio increases dramatically at the start of GBE phase, resulting in effective incompressibility of apical surface of cells.
source: Indeed, quantitative comparison with an independently measured flow field (Figure 1c–e) shows that the ν20 /ν27 ratio increases dramatically at the start of GBE phase (corresponding to the relative increase of the underlying 2D bulk modulus, see Appendix 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) resulting in effective incompressibility of apical surface of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the ratio of viscosities shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The temporal coincidence between completion of cellularization and increase of the bulk modulus provides an intriguing possible explanation of how the continuous transition in the time dependent variable might be realized.
source: The temporal coincidence between completion of cellularization and increase of the bulk modulus provides an intriguing possible explanation of how the continuous transition in our time dependent variable might be realized.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temporal correlation between cellularization and the change in bulk modulus.

claim: In twist mutants, DV asymmetry of the basal myosin pool is strongly reduced in comparison to WT during early flow phases.
source: During early flow phases – corresponding to times of pre-VF flow in WT – DV asymmetry of the basal myosin pool is strongly reduced in comparison to WT, as is tissue movement towards the dorsal pole (Figure 4b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of basal myosin asymmetry in WT and twist mutants shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In twist mutants, tissue movement towards the dorsal pole is reduced compared to WT during early flow phases.
source: During early flow phases – corresponding to times of pre-VF flow in WT – DV asymmetry of the basal myosin pool is strongly reduced in comparison to WT, as is tissue movement towards the dorsal pole (Figure 4b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flow field data in twist mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In twist mutants, anisotropy of the apical myosin pool increases at a slower rate as compared to WT.
source: Moreover, anisotropy of the apical myosin pool increases at a slower rate as compared to WT. As previously reported for strain rates (Butler et al., 2009), this is most pronounced for the first 20 min (Figure 4c, compare Figure 4 – fig. supplement = 0 with Figure 2—figure supplement 3e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of apical myosin anisotropy in WT and twist mutants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In bcd nos tsl embryos, the early basal DV asymmetry is similar to WT, with only slightly reduced myosin asymmetries and dorsal movement.
source: In bcd nos tsl (bnt) embryos lacking all AP patterning, the early basal DV asymmetry is similar to WT, with only slightly reduced myosin asymmetries and dorsal movement (Figure 4b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of basal myosin asymmetry in WT and bnt mutants shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In bcd nos tsl embryos at later stages, anisotropy of the apical myosin pool remains low and comparable to pre-VF WT levels.
source: At later stages, however, anisotropy of the apical myosin pool remains low and comparable to pre-VF WT levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of apical myosin anisotropy in WT and bnt mutants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The low apical myosin anisotropy in bcd nos tsl embryos is expected given the uniform expression of pair-rule genes in a bnt genetic background.
source: This result is expected given the uniform expression of pair-rule genes in a bnt genetic background (Blankenship et al., 2006) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Blankenship et al., 2006.

claim: The basal myosin pool forms an isotropic and contiguous network.
source: We propose that the basal myosin pool forms an isotropic and contiguous network (He et al., 2016), contracting in a similar fashion as purified actomyosin gels in vitro (Bendix et al., 2008; Alvarado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Imbalance within the basal myosin network, caused by the twist dependent depletion of myosin on the ventral side, drives global dorsal-ward flow in the pre-VF phase.
source: Imbalance within this network, caused by the twi dependent depletion of myosin on the ventral side, drives global dorsal-ward flow in the pre-VF phase, which continues to contribute until early GBE (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in silico perturbation analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Local depletion of basal myosin on the ventral side has a global effect, most evidently manifested by a 'sink' on the dorsal side.
source: Interestingly, in silico perturbations indicate the local depletion (on the ventral side) has a global effect, most evidently manifested by a 'sink' on the dorsal side, which is lost in a simulation using the same parameters as WT, but no DV modulation of the basal myosin pool (Figure 4d, left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in silico perturbation analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: There is a striking gradient of anisotropic apical myosin along the DV axis, reaching highest levels in lateral ectoderm and lowest levels in amnioserosa tissue at the dorsal pole.
source: In addition to previously described accumulation of isotropic myosin in ventral regions (Martin et al., 2009), we observe a striking gradient of anisotropic apical myosin along the DV axis, reaching highest levels in lateral ectoderm and lowest levels in amnioserosa tissue at the dorsal pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by the myosin distribution data shown in the figures.

claim: The modulation of myosin distribution is critical for the dynamics because the force driving the flow arises from the non-uniformity of the stress.
source: Because the force driving the flow arises from the non-uniformity of the stress, this modulation of myosin distribution is critical for the dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the continuum mechanics model and the in silico perturbation analysis.

claim: The local rate of strain is a result of the tissue-wide distribution of forces generated by the spatial non-uniformity of myosin.
source: While local rate of cell intercalation is often interpreted in terms of local myosin distribution on cellular and sub-cellular scales, our model shows that the local rate of strain is a result of the tissue-wide distribution of forces generated by the spatial non-uniformity of myosin (mathematically described by the divergence of the myosin tensor) (Figure 4d, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results and in silico perturbations shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The importance of spatial modulation suggests a novel role of the dorsal signaling pathway in generation of GBE flow.
source: The importance of spatial modulation (Figure 4d) suggests a novel role of the dorsal signaling pathway in generation of GBE flow.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the importance of spatial modulation demonstrated in the modeling.

claim: In twist mutants, both the rate of increase as well as the peak myosin anisotropy are significantly reduced in the first 20 min of GBE flow.
source: Surprisingly, in twi mutants both the rate of increase as well as the peak myosin anisotropy are significantly reduced in the first 20 min of GBE flow (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of myosin anisotropy in WT and twist mutants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The reduced intercalation and strain rates observed in twist mutants has been previously reported.
source: The reduced intercalation and strain rates observed in these mutants has been previously reported (Butler et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Butler et al., 2009.

claim: The model accounts for the reduced rate of strain in twist mutants in terms of the changes in spatial distribution and the reduced level of myosin anisotropy.
source: Our model accounts for the reduced rate of strain in terms of the changes in spatial distribution and the reduced level of myosin anisotropy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of twist mutants.

claim: Elimination of twist expression in the ventral mesoderm may affect myosin anisotropy in the lateral ectoderm through mechanical feedback on myosin recruitment.
source: This however brings up the question of how elimination of twi expression in the ventral mesoderm affects myosin anisotropy in the lateral ectoderm. We suggest that this effect may be due to mechanical feedback on myosin recruitment, which relates the later to local rate of strain.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the non-local effects of twist mutation.

claim: Through 'dynamic recruitment' effect, changes in the ventral region that modify global flow patterns can affect myosin distribution and anisotropy in the lateral region.
source: Through this 'dynamic recruitment' effect (Noll et al., 2017; Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009), changes in the ventral region that modify global flow patterns can affect myosin distribution and anisotropy in the lateral region.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Local modification of the myosin pattern can produce not only a non-local perturbation of the flow, but also a non-local perturbation of myosin distribution.
source: In this way, local modification of the myosin pattern can produce not only a non-local perturbation of the flow, but also a non-local perturbation of myosin distribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanical feedback mechanism.

claim: The transition towards areal incompressibility at the onset of GBE-flow, together with reduced polarization kinetics and reduced strain rates observed in twist mutants, indicates that non-local consequences of stress generated largely in lateral ectoderm can account for the dorsal movement of the posterior midgut.
source: The global nature of the flow is reinforced by the observed transition towards areal incompressibility at the onset of GBE-flow, which together with reduced polarization kinetics and reduced strain rates observed in twi mutants, indicates that non-local consequences of stress generated largely in lateral ectoderm can account for the dorsal movement of the posterior midgut.
evidence: This is an interpretation that integrates multiple observations from the study.

claim: Morphogenetic flow is a global response to local forcing which arises from the spatial modulation of myosin density and anisotropy.
source: Taken together, our observations show that morphogenetic flow is a global response to local forcing which arises from the spatial modulation of myosin density and anisotropy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the modeling and experimental results.

claim: Myosin anisotropy is derived from the spatial patterns of developmental transcription factors.
source: The latter is derived from the spatial patterns of developmental transcription factors, but we suggest may also involve mechanical feedback affecting recruitment of myosin.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about pair-rule gene patterning and a speculative hypothesis about mechanical feedback.

claim: Mechanical feedback may affect recruitment of myosin.
source: The latter is derived from the spatial patterns of developmental transcription factors, but we suggest may also involve mechanical feedback affecting recruitment of myosin.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed in the discussion.

claim: The quantitative approach provides a framework for integrating the effect of local factors in the description of the global flow.
source: Our quantitative approach provides a framework for integrating the effect of local factors in the description of the global flow.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.
